blogs.title: From ‘Right to Control’ to Fraudulent Inducement: How the Fifth Circuit Reframed Social-Media Pump-and-Dump Prosecutions
blogs.description: This post would analyze the Fifth Circuit’s central move: treating the indictment not as an impermissible right-to-control case under Ciminelli, but as a classic fraudulent-inducement prosecution after Kousisis. It would explain why the court viewed the alleged misstatements as aimed at inducing followers to part with money to buy securities, and why that distinction matters for the future of federal fraud doctrine.

blogs.title: Property Without Loss? The Fifth Circuit’s Broad Reading of ‘Intent to Defraud’ After Kousisis
blogs.description: This post would focus on the opinion’s most important doctrinal implication: the government need not allege that defendants sought to leave victims economically worse off, only that they schemed to obtain money or property by deception. It would explore the tension between requiring a traditional property interest and simultaneously allowing prosecutions where victims received market-value securities, asking whether the court has embraced an especially expansive conception of fraud injury.

blogs.title: Section 1348 Grows Up: What the Fifth Circuit’s Opinion Says About Securities Fraud as a Mail-and-Wire-Fraud Cousin
blogs.description: This post would examine the court’s methodology in borrowing heavily from mail and wire fraud precedents to interpret 18 U.S.C. § 1348. It would consider whether that cross-pollination is textually and structurally sound, and how the opinion fits into a broader trend of treating § 1348 as a flexible anti-fraud backstop rather than a tightly securities-specific criminal provision.

blogs.title: Finfluencers, Market Manipulation, and Criminal Law: The Emerging Case Against Online Trading Hype
blogs.description: This post would situate the case in the broader enforcement campaign against social-media-based trading schemes. It would discuss how the court’s reasoning lowers pleading obstacles in prosecutions of online personalities who allegedly conceal their own positions while touting stocks, and how the decision may shape the line between aggressive market commentary, deceptive promotion, and criminal securities fraud.

blogs.title: An Indictment-Friendly Opinion: What the Fifth Circuit Signals About Pretrial Challenges to Fraud Charges
blogs.description: This post would analyze the procedural posture and the court’s insistence that, at the indictment stage, allegations must be taken as true so long as each material element is adequately pleaded. It would argue that the opinion is as much about criminal procedure as substantive fraud law, reinforcing a judicial reluctance to resolve close factual questions about materiality, inducement, and investor injury on a motion to dismiss.
